We have seasons because Earth's spin axis is tilted about 23.4° compared with the plane of its orbit, and the axis keeps pointing the same way in space as Earth goes around the Sun [1][2]. So for part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and six months later the Southern Hemisphere does. The hemisphere leaning toward the Sun gets sunlight from higher in the sky. That light hits the ground more directly, so its energy is concentrated on a smaller area. Days are also longer, so the ground heats up more and it's summer [1][3]. The hemisphere leaning away gets low-angle sunlight that spreads over a larger area, plus short days, and that's winter [3].

A common belief is that seasons come from Earth's distance to the Sun changing, but that's not the cause. The distance only varies by about 3%, and Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the Northern Hemisphere's winter [1][2]. The fact that the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time also shows that tilt is what matters.
